new_statements.quote: The accentual systems of all other Bs dialects have phonetic details involving both vowel length and stress. The vowel in an accented open penult (CV́) is long: all dialects (but Kuy and Tsg) bátaq → bá:taq young. [...] In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult [CVC.CV(C)] are accented on the penult (see 10.2.1.). [p.216:] All Bs speech varieties except some dialects of Kuy and Tsg retain phonemic accent. The following minimal pair is found in all dialects and establishes contrastive accent for PBS: punuq [pú:nuq] tree trunk < PBS *púnuq and punuq [punúq] full < PBS *punúq.
new_statements.citation: Zorc, R. David Paul. 1977. The Bisayan dialects of the Philippines: subgrouping and reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44. new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (stress plus penult length) is lexically contrastive between the penult and the final syllable of the stem (pú:nuq 'tree trunk' vs punúq 'full'; Dsp ráhaq 'cooked' vs raháq 'cook'); it is predictable only when the penult is closed, in which case the penult is always stressed. An accented open penult is long; ultima vowels are short. Affixes belong to accent classes that keep, shift to penult, shift to ultima, or reverse the base accent (§4.2). Zorc's 1967 primer for the same Loocnon-Alcantaranon variety gives the pedagogical default: unmarked words are accented on the penult, marked words on the ultima (HAMPÁNGAN vs HAMPANGÁN).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for these dialects; Zorc adds that stress also serves as a phrase-level 'syntactic feature, a means of counting the full words in a clause' and that stress (not length) can shift under exclamatory intonation (p.50-51).
new_statements.exceptions: Statement is pan-Bisayan ('all other Bs dialects', 36 dialects incl. Lok, Alc, Dsp) with Kuyonon and Tausug excepted; closed-penult rule excepted only for Kuyonon; loanwords and accent-pair verbs/statives noted (p.218).
new_statements.domain_note: Word (stem/derivative) accent in citation forms; Zorc distinguishes contrastive length on the penult from clause-level stress placement, which intonation can override. No Inonhan-specific example appears on pp.50/216; Dispoholnon examples appear in the accent-pair list on p.218 and Loocnon examples with acute marks in Zorc 1967 dialogs.
new_statements.identity_note: Inonhan (inon1237, ISO loc; also Inunhan, Onhan, Loocnon) = Zorc 1977's Looknon (Lok; Look & Santa Fe, Tablas, 'other name Inunhan'), Alcantaranon (Alc; Alcantara) and Dispoholnon (Dsp; San Andres/Despujols), i.e. his North-Central West Bisayan node (Zorc 2022: 'INUNHAN... corresponds to the NORTH-CENTRAL node of the West Bisayan branch'), which also includes the Mindoro migrant variety Bulalakawnon (Blk). Zorc 1967's 'LG. (Loocnon-Alcantaranon)' is the same variety. The deciding statement is pan-Bisayan ('all other Bs dialects' minus Kuyonon/Tausug) with Lok/Alc/Dsp included by name in the dialect inventory, not an Inonhan-only description.

sources.note: Bibliography only: two descriptive refs (van den Heuvel 1997, Zorc 1967); subclassification per Zorc 1977.

No phonology section; lists towns (San Andres, Santa Maria, Alcantara, Ferrol, Looc, Santa Fe; Carabao I.; migrants in Mindoro) and the 1999 NT; numerals printed with acute accents (Isyá, Darwá, Tatló, Limá, Pitó, Waló, Siyám, Púlô) but no rule stated.
